sources.text:
«Des sentiments très mitigés» : départ du chef d'une institution culturelle américaine dans le viseur de Trump
Ce départ survient alors que la Maison-Blanche a multiplié les attaques à l’encontre de la Smithsonian Institution, emblématique complexe de musées américains, qu’elle accuse de véhiculer une vision du monde trop progressiste.
Passer la publicité Passer la publicité
Le chef de la Smithsonian Institution, emblématique complexe de musées américains, a annoncé mardi son départ, sur fond de vives pressions de l'administration Trump pour réécrire l'histoire américaine présentée par l'organisation. «C'est avec des sentiments très mitigés et une profonde gratitude que j'annonce mon départ à la retraite de la Smithsonian», a écrit dans un communiqué Lonnie Bunch, premier Afro-Américain à avoir occupé ce poste.
Cet historien de 73 ans avait pris la tête de la Smithsonian Institution en 2019 après plus de trois décennies de travail au sein de ce vaste complexe muséal, éducatif et de recherche, régi par un partenariat public-privé unique en son genre. M. Bunch avait notamment contribué à la création du Musée national de l'histoire et de la culture afro-américaines à Washington.
Passer la publicité
Son départ survient alors que la Maison-Blanche a multiplié les attaques à l'encontre de l'institution, qu'elle accuse de véhiculer une vision du monde trop progressiste. En août 2025, Donald Trump l'avait accusée d'être «HORS DE CONTRÔLE», et avait déploré que les musées de la capitale fédérale présentent selon lui une image «horrible de notre pays, (notamment) sur les méfaits de l'esclavage (...) et rien sur sa réussite et son éclat».
Pression de Trump ?
Le président républicain a ensuite signé en mars 2026 un décret visant à reprendre le contrôle du contenu de ces musées. Dans un document de 162 pages ensuite publié par la Maison-Blanche, l'administration Trump accuse notamment la Smithsonian Institution de ne pas suffisamment souligner «le rôle central de la foi chrétienne» dans l'histoire américaine. «Les Américains blancs, les hommes et les chrétiens sont régulièrement dénigrés comme l'incarnation des structures oppressives», peut-on lire dans ce texte.
Cette pression s'est récemment accentuée en août, quand un ministre de Trump a écrit au conseil d'administration de l'institution pour réclamer une réunion sur ces accusations d'«idéologie radicale», la menaçant à l'occasion de la priver de fonds publics.
«Je dois être honnête, ça a été stressant», a confié Lonnie Bunch au New York Times, tout en assurant que ces pressions n'étaient pour autant pas à l'origine de sa décision de partir. «C'était simplement le moment», a-t-il affirmé.

sources.news_title: Smithsonian Leader Behind Leftward Degradation Resigns
sources.text:
Lonnie Bunch, the secretary of the Smithsonian Institution who led its leftward degradation, resigned Tuesday after years of overseeing the advancement of anti-American propaganda at the nation’s premier art, culture, and history establishment.
Bunch, who took over as secretary in 2019 but has been at the Smithsonian for almost 38 years, founded the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture prior to becoming secretary. Under his leadership, the Smithsonian added to its insidious track record of partitioning its museums along racial and gender ideology lines. He plans to leave the Smithsonian by the end of the year, according to the resignation announcement.
Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, who is chancellor of the Smithsonian by law, lauded Bunch’s tenure in a statement reacting to the resignation, saying, “Secretary Bunch has pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story. The Regents, and the Smithsonian, have benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership.” However, as The Federalist has chronicled, the Smithsonian has been in stark decline for years.
For example, the National Museum of American History’s director, Anthea Hartig, has repeatedly parroted a land acknowledgment claiming that the United States is on stolen land taken from American Indian tribes. A video from the institution called “The Indian Problem” asserts that the American government committed genocide against American Indians.
As John Fonte noted in these pages, Bunch and Hartig “consistently claim that they are presenting a nuanced, neutral, unbiased narrative of America’s story to our citizens and foreign visitors.” But they actually use the “crude weaponized concept” of “stolen land” to “‘problematize’ our founding (to use Anthea Hartig’s own language) and, in the process, de-legitimize historic America. This is all part of the effort to fundamentally transform our nation.”
The American History Museum also referred to the founding of America and civilizational expansion as the “profound unsettling of the continent.”
That kind of propaganda, and much more, has been ingrained in the Smithsonian for a long time. The institution partnered with the far-left historical revisionism group the Zinn Education Project (ZEP) to participate in “teach-ins” for teachers to receive continuing education credit.
One of the ZEP’s initiatives has been to abolish Columbus Day, and it has been partially successful, especially at the state and local levels. President Joe Biden officially proclaimed the protest “holiday” of Indigenous Peoples’ Day every year he was in office.
ZEP also advances fake, anti-American histories about the American Founding and Revolution, slavery, the Civil War, World War II, and demonizes the anti-communists in the House Un-American Activities Committee while shielding the role of communism in the American labor movement and civil rights movement.
The Smithsonian also promoted homosexuality and argued that “transgender” athletes should be allowed to compete against members of the opposite sex, denying that characteristics like testosterone and bone density give men an advantage over women.
Meanwhile, the American flag is seen either being used to support left-wing causes like mass migration and LGBT material, or it is being burnt, associated with the Ku Klux Klan, or included with other anti-American exhibits.
At every turn, in seemingly every museum, there is anti-American propaganda that is meant to serve as the “memory for the nation,” as the Smithsonian itself claims to be.
The Museum of African Art used exhibits to advance Black Lives Matter and the “national racial reckoning” narrative, and showed an exhibit putting drug overdose victim George Floyd and communist revolutionary Che Guevara on par with Jesus Christ.
The Museum of Natural History had a display showing how cell phone footage, like in the case of George Floyd, can be used to start riots and protests in order to advance social justice.
The Museum of Asian Art highlighted “transgenderism” with an exhibit “confront[ing] notions of gender and cultural identity through photography” to “explore representations of power, place, and sexuality in today’s world.”
The institutional capture was so thorough that soon after taking office, the Trump administration started its push to revitalize the Smithsonian, aiming to restore it to its founding mission: to be “an establishment for the increase and diffusion of knowledge among men.”
“A healthy attachment to this country is neither blind to its flaws nor fanatical in believing that America is the source of all good,” Hillsdale College’s Matthew Spalding testified to Congress earlier this year, noting how Smithsonian bureaucrats “killed America’s story.” “Nevertheless, each generation should be equipped with a knowledge of America’s principles and history, a reverence for their liberties, and a reflective love of their country. That patriotism must be strong enough and unsentimental enough to coexist with criticism, dissent, disappointment, and opposition. But it is love all the same.”

sources.news_title: Smithsonian leader Lonnie G. Bunch to retire
sources.text:
The Smithsonian Institution has announced the retirement of its secretary, Lonnie G. Bunch III, following seven years in the top role—the first African American and the first historian to hold the position. The 73-year-old Bunch will have spent a total of 38 years working at the Smithsonian in various capacities, 11 of those as the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture (NMAAHC).
“It is with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude that I announce my retirement from the Smithsonian,” Bunch said in a statement on Tuesday (8 September). “I have spent nearly half of my life working at and being part of the Smithsonian family, and what a privilege it has been. There is no place like the Smithsonian—it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together. I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.”
Bunch’s Smithsonian tenure began in 1978 at the National Air and Space Museum. He would later move to the National Museum of American History, where he became the associate director of curatorial affairs. After leaving for a four-year stint as the president of the Chicago Historical Society, Bunch came back to lead the NMAAHC in 2005. He became the Smithsonian secretary in 2019.
As a historian, Bunch has published more than a dozen books on African American history, US presidents and museums. His most recent book is A Fool's Errand: Creating the National Museum of African American History and Culture in the Age of Bush, Obama and Trump (2019).
Bunch has also received numerous awards and honours, including France’s Legion of Honour, the W.E.B. Du Bois Medal and lifetime achievement awards from both the American Alliance of Museums and the African American Association of Museums.
“I have had the honour of working with Lonnie Bunch for more than two decades,” Franklin D. Raines, the chair of the Smithsonian’s board of regents, said in a statement. “I have seen firsthand how Secretary Bunch’s leadership of our 21 museums and the National Zoo has illuminated the nation’s past, opened pathways to new knowledge and powered creativity and innovation. These efforts will help create a better shared future for all.”
Raines added that the board will soon announce an acting secretary and announce a national search for a new leader.
Bunch leaves the Smithsonian's helm as the Trump administration continues to attack its programming and leadership with accusations of “wokeness”. Ever since Trump began his second presidential term in early 2025, he has attempted to re-shape the institution to align with his own politics—largely through executive orders and public battles with museum leadership.
Yet throughout all the turmoil, Bunch has remained cool-headed and diplomatic, treading the line between unwavering support of his staff and professionally responding to the Trump administration’s often outrageous accusations. However, Bunch has said that his retirement is not a result of political clashes.
“It is time for my next chapter, a chapter that will allow me to continue to protect the integrity of the Smithsonian and to champion the importance of a history that illuminates and celebrates the complex story of our nation,” Bunch’s statement continued. “The Smithsonian has been a reservoir of science, history, art and culture that freely allows the public to find knowledge, understanding, clarity, education, hope and a bit of joy. I will always carry the Smithsonian within me.”

Head of Smithsonian museums announces he will be stepping down
The US institution is under pressure from the Trump administration to change how it portrays the country’s history.
The head of the Smithsonian Institution will be stepping down from his position by the end of the year, following pressure from the administration of United States President Donald Trump.
In a statement on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch announced he was leaving the institution, an organisation that oversees one of the world’s largest collections of museums and educational and research centres.

- list 2 of 3Trump says Smithsonian museums only cover ‘how bad Slavery was’ in US
- list 3 of 3Why is Trump going after the Smithsonian museums?
“I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward,” Bunch said.
“It is time for my next chapter, a chapter that will allow me to continue to protect the integrity of the Smithsonian and to champion the importance of a history that illuminates and celebrates the complex story of our nation.”
Many of the Smithsonian’s museums occupy a place of pride on the National Mall in Washington, DC.
But since the start of Trump’s second term as US president, the institution has come under increasing fire from conservatives who object to its depictions of racism, colonialism and other aspects of US history.
While the Smithsonian does not fall under the president’s direct authority, a large part of its budget comes from the federal government, and the Trump administration has threatened to sever that funding stream over the institution’s alleged “anti-American ideology”.
In July, Trump had ordered the US Department of the Interior to erect “warning signs” near the entrance to the National Museum of American History to inform visitors about the museum’s alleged bias.
In August, the Interior Department also sent a letter to the Smithsonian detailing its criticism if the institution did not address its concerns by changing its top leadership.
“Because these concerns arise from executive leadership and institutional ideology at the Smithsonian, the appropriate response must likewise address executive leadership and institutional ideology,” the letter said.
‘American exceptionalism’
The Smithsonian museums are free for the public to visit, and they draw millions of people each year.
They include the National Air and Space Museum, National Museum of American History, National Museum of the American Indian, National Museum of Natural History and National Portrait Gallery.
Bunch was appointed as the secretary of the Smithsonian in 2019, becoming the first African American to serve at the helm of the 180-year-old institution.
He previously served as director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, which opened in 2016 after a years-long effort.
But the Trump administration has sought to crack down on institutions it accuses of promoting left-wing “woke” ideology and movements like diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), a social justice initiative to encourage the participation of marginalised groups.
As part of that effort, Trump has sought to exert greater control over programming at cultural institutions like the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, one of the US capital’s most prominent theatre venues.
He has also ordered probes of other entities, from schools and universities to the military and national parks, in an effort to rid federally supported institutions of what he called “discriminatory” DEI practices.
The Smithsonian, however, was an early target of the Trump administration’s anti-DEI campaign.
Within months of taking office in 2025, Trump issued an executive order titled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History”, which called for changes to ensure the Smithsonian returned to its “rightful place as a symbol of inspiration and American greatness”.
The White House, at the time, accused the Smithsonian’s American Art Museum and National Museum of African American History and Culture of promoting narratives that portrayed US values as harmful and oppressive.
In May 2025, Trump also said he had fired Kim Sajet, the director of the National Portrait Gallery, a Smithsonian museum, after he accused her of being a “highly partisan person, and a strong supporter of DEI, which is totally inappropriate for her position”.
Critics, however, argued that Trump did not have the authority to fire Sajet, who resigned under pressure in June of that year.
Further controversies erupted when the Smithsonian removed references to Trump’s two first-term impeachments from exhibits, before reversing course amid public outcry.
Soon after, in August 2025, the White House wrote to Bunch’s office saying it would conduct a review of the museum’s content, including its exhibits and social media content, to ensure the narratives shared would “celebrate American exceptionalism”.
Bunch has remained under pressure since that time, facing the prospect of balancing the institution’s funding requirements with the need to shield itself from political interference.
In the wake of his resignation on Tuesday, historians and artists like director Ken Burns voiced their support for the outgoing Smithsonian head.
“Lonnie Bunch is a great historian, public servant and a dear friend,” Burns wrote on social media.
“He has devoted his career to helping us understand the full American story in all its complexity. Our country is better for his work, and I am deeply grateful for it.”

Smithsonian secretary to retire as Trump exerts control over institution
Washington (United States) (AFP) – The head of the Smithsonian Institution is set to retire, amid an unprecedented drive by President Donald Trump to reshape the treasured museum and research complex he has faulted over its presentation of American history and values.
Issued on:
Lonnie G. Bunch III -- the first Black person and first historian to serve in the role -- said Tuesday he had "very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude" as he announced his departure by the end of 2026 following seven years in the top job and nearly 38 at the institution overall.
The 73-year-old was named secretary in June 2019, a position that made him leader of the world's largest museum, education and research complex. His career accomplishments include founding the National Museum of African American History and Culture and authoring numerous books, including one on the NMAAHC's creation.
Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as the Smithsonian Chancellor, hailed his "distinguished service," adding: "Secretary Bunch has pursued excellence in the telling of our nation's story."
Trump and fellow Republicans in Congress have accused the Smithsonian -- created by the federal government in 1846 but which operates in a unique position outside any branch of government -- of being beholden to liberal "woke" ideology.
A 162-page White House report said that Smithsonian leadership has "consistently denigrated and displaced whites, males, Christians, and Americans in educational materials and programming," and in July the president issued an order to install signage warning visitors about "ideological capture" near the National Museum of American History.
The pressure continued in an August 28 letter by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to the Smithsonian's board of regents -- bypassing Bunch while calling for an in-person meeting to address its accusations of "radical ideology."
Co-signed by Vince Haley, the White House domestic policy chief, it added the government "cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership."
In May 2025, Trump announced he had fired the director of the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, calling her "a highly partisan person."
The Smithsonian asserted it had control over personnel matters, but Sajet later resigned, citing the museum's best interests.
Trump is also engaged in an ongoing tussle about having his name appear on the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, with the administration adding Trump's name to the facade.
A court ordered his name removed, and while the letters have come down, the president's handpicked board members resisted, voting in August to add the words "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump" beneath Kennedy's name.
The administration has also warned in a court filing the storied arts venue may have to be demolished if courts block the president's plans to overhaul the landmark.

sources.news_title: With Bunch set to depart Smithsonian, Democrats urge ‘full history’
sources.text:
With Bunch set to depart Smithsonian, Democrats urge ‘full history’
Congress reacts as secretary says he has decided to leave
As Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced he will be leaving his role by the end of the year, Democrats in Congress praised him for trying to show the “full history” of America.
Bunch was the first African American and the first historian to be appointed to the role. He has led the institution during a fraught time, as it faces ongoing pressure to conform its content to the White House’s vision.
“I have spent nearly half of my life working at and being part of the Smithsonian family, and what a privilege it has been,” Bunch said in a statement Tuesday. “I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.”
Bunch has worked for the Smithsonian since 1978, when he joined the institution as an educational specialist at the National Air and Space Museum. He went on to become the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture and was appointed by the Smithsonian Board of Regents to lead the broader institution in 2019.
“One of my goals as Secretary was for the Smithsonian to increase our reach in education, in scholarship, in scientific research. I believe we should be in every home and classroom in the country,” Bunch testified in December 2023 at a House Administration Committee oversight hearing.
While House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., did not release a statement Tuesday afternoon on Bunch’s coming departure, at least one Democratic member of the panel weighed in.
“I’m grateful for his decades of service and his commitment to telling the full, honest story of our nation,” Rep. Terri A. Sewell, D-Ala., wrote on X, calling his leadership “trailblazing.”
Sewell and other Democrats in Congress have accused President Donald Trump of trying to rope the Smithsonian into broader culture wars and erase uncomfortable truths, like slavery and colonization, from American history.
A 162-page White House report released this summer complained of “ideological capture” at the National Museum of American History, following an executive order last March that called for the removal of “divisive, race-centered ideology” across the Smithsonian’s 21 museums and the National Zoo.
Some Republicans in Congress, like Rep. Keith Self of Texas, Rep. Tim Burchett of Tennessee and Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana, introduced bills to codify the action by Trump, but those have so far seen no movement. Lawmakers have mostly stayed on the sidelines of the fight, aside from two different congressional hearings this summer.
Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto, D-Nev., one of six members of Congress who sit on the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, said Bunch had served with “distinction.”
“He is a student of history who has devoted his life to telling America’s full history and cultivating our nation’s continued love of learning and exploration,” she said in a statement.
One of the congressional Republicans serving on the board, Rep. Carlos Gimenez, R-Fla., said in a statement, “I look forward to working with my fellow Regents as the Smithsonian begins this important new chapter and searches for a new Secretary who will preserve America’s history and master the art of storytelling for generations to come.”
The Smithsonian receives roughly two-thirds of its funding from federal sources. Last appropriations cycle, the president’s budget requested a cut of 12 percent, but Congress opted to keep the funding level mostly steady at just over $1 billion.
“Secretary Bunch has guided the Smithsonian through a period of unprecedented political interference while remaining committed to scholarship, expertise, and the public trust,” House Interior-Environment Appropriations Subcommittee ranking member Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, said in a statement.
Board of Regents Chair Franklin D. Raines announced Tuesday that the board would name an acting secretary “in due course” and begin a “national search” for Bunch’s replacement.
Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., ranking member of the Senate Rules and Administration panel, said Bunch “spoke truth to power” in the face of Trump’s “attacks” on the Smithsonian.
“While I respect his decision to depart, the job now falls to the Board of Regents and Congress to ensure the success of his work will remain for generations to come,” Padilla said in a statement.

sources.news_title: Who is Lonnie Bunch? Smithsonian chief retiring amid Trump admin strife
sources.text:
Lonnie G. Bunch III, the first Black secretary of the Smithsonian Institution and one of the most influential museum leaders in the United States, announced Tuesday that he will step down at the end of 2026 after seven years leading the nation's largest museum complex.
His departure comes after a tumultuous year in which President Donald Trump's administration intensified scrutiny of the Smithsonian, accusing some museum leaders of promoting politically biased interpretations of American history amid the nation's 250th anniversary celebrations. The Smithsonian said Bunch would leave his post at the end of the year after serving as secretary since 2019.
"I depart with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude," Bunch said in a statement announcing his retirement.
Newsweek has reached out to the White House via email on Tuesday afternoon for comment.
Calling Bunch "a student of history" who devoted his life to telling "America's full history," Senator Catherine Cortez Masto, a Nevada Democrat and member of the Smithsonian Board of Regents, praised his more than 30 years of service to the Smithsonian. In a statement shared with Newsweek via email, Cortez Masto said she hopes the institution's next secretary will demonstrate the same commitment to arts, culture, science and history.
Smithsonian Chief Lonnie Bunch Announces Retirement at 73
Bunch, 73, is a historian, author and longtime museum executive who has spent more than four decades in the museum field.
Before becoming secretary of the Smithsonian in 2019, he was best known as the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, D.C. Under his leadership, the museum opened in 2016 after years of planning and fundraising and quickly became one of the Smithsonian's most visited institutions.
His appointment as secretary marked a historic milestone for the Smithsonian. Bunch became the first African American to lead the institution in its nearly 180-year history.
As secretary, he oversaw a sprawling enterprise that includes 21 museums, the National Zoo, major research centers and educational programs that draw millions of visitors annually.
Bunch's path to the top of the Smithsonian began in New Jersey, where he was born in Newark and raised in nearby Belleville. A trained historian, he attended Howard University before earning bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees in American and African American history from American University.
After beginning his career at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum, Bunch went on to hold leadership positions at museums in California, Chicago and Washington before becoming the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture and, later, the first Black and first historian to lead the Smithsonian Institution.
Why Is Bunch Leaving Now?
The Smithsonian did not cite a specific reason for Bunch's departure beyond his decision to retire.
However, his announcement comes amid unprecedented pressure from the Trump administration.
In July, a White House report sharply criticized Smithsonian leadership, particularly officials at the National Museum of American History, accusing them of advancing ideological interpretations of the nation's past. The report said some museum leaders could not be trusted to present American history in a manner that was "inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic."
The administration later increased pressure on the institution. In August, Trump directed officials to install signs outside the National Museum of American History informing visitors that some exhibits were allegedly inaccurate, a move that prompted pushback from museum leadership. The White House had argued that the museum failed to present history "in a way that is inspiring, unifying, and worthy of our great republic."
Anthea Hartig, director of the National Museum of American History, rejected that characterization during congressional testimony, telling lawmakers that the White House report "does not fairly or accurately characterize the full body of work at the museum."
Trump Admin Threatens to Revoke Funding for Smithsonian
The tensions stem from a broader effort by Trump to influence how federal institutions present American history as the country prepares to celebrate its 250th anniversary in 2026.
In March 2025, Trump signed an executive order titled "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History," arguing that some cultural institutions had engaged in efforts to "rewrite" the nation's past.
The administration's efforts extended beyond museum exhibits. Trump also proposed reducing federal support for some Smithsonian programs and directed agencies to review public-facing historical content across museums, parks and other cultural sites.
The order specifically referenced the National Museum of African American History and Culture and sparked reviews of exhibitions, educational materials and public-facing content across federal cultural institutions.
Later, the White House launched a wider review of Smithsonian museums and exhibits, directing officials to evaluate whether content aligned with what the administration described as American ideals and values.
The review initially targeted eight Smithsonian museums, including the National Museum of American History, the National Museum of African American History and Culture, the National Portrait Gallery and the National Air and Space Museum. The review extended to the National Museum of Natural History, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, and the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden.
The March executive order's reach extended beyond Smithsonian museums. It prompted changes at National Park Service sites, including the removal or revision of some exhibits and interpretive signs, as the administration sought to align federal historical presentations with its vision for the nation's 250th anniversary.
In June, the Trump administration was ordered to restore signs and exhibits at national parks covering topics such as slavery, climate change and Indigenous history, with a federal judge ruling that their removal set "a dangerous precedent of censorship and sanitization."
What's Next for the Smithsonian
Despite the administration's pressure campaign, the Smithsonian operates independently of the executive branch.
Museum directors report to the secretary, while overall oversight comes from the Smithsonian Board of Regents, whose members include Vice President JD Vance, Chief Justice John Roberts, members of Congress and citizen regents.
Because of that structure, Trump does not have direct authority to fire Smithsonian leaders in the same way he has reshaped other cultural institutions, including the Kennedy Center.
Roberts, who serves as the Smithsonian's chancellor, praised Bunch's tenure following the announcement.
"He has pursued excellence in the telling of our nation's story," Roberts said in a statement.
Bunch's retirement now sets up a high-stakes search for his successor, one that will unfold as the Smithsonian remains at the center of a national debate over how American history should be presented to the public.
The Associated Press contributed to this story.
Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas

Smithsonian chief Lonnie Bunch to resign amid Trump attacks
After a seven-year run marked most recently by attacks from the Trump administration, Lonnie Bunch III announced today that he was stepping down as secretary of the Smithsonian.
The White House has escalated its criticism of how the Smithsonian presents American history and values, prompting concern from some about what they see as an assault on the institution’s autonomy and commendation from others for reining in an organization they view as overtaken by liberal bias.
In an interview, Bunch, 73, said it was not the pressure that had led to his departure.
“It was really just saying, now’s the time,” he said.
“I’m a fighter,” he added.
At the same time, he acknowledged the strain of the role.

“I have to be honest, it has been stressful,” he said. “And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”
In a statement, Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, said that Bunch had “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story” and that the Smithsonian had “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership.” The Smithsonian said Bunch was expected to depart at the end of the year.
For more than a year, Bunch has tried to balance diplomacy and openness to criticism with a determination to resist a White House push to present what President Donald Trump calls “patriotic” history. Some admire how Bunch has managed to quietly hold the line against the White House. Others believe the Smithsonian has shown too much deference to Trump and even engaged in self-censorship.
Last year, painter Amy Sherald withdrew her blockbuster show at the National Portrait Gallery over a disagreement about how the museum would display her portrait of a transgender Statue of Liberty.
But Bunch said he had no regrets. “My goal has been to win, not to make me feel good,” he said. “To win — to protect the Smithsonian — there were times I would fight, make clear what the red lines were. And there were other times I let things go.”
Bunch, a widely respected historian who previously oversaw the creation of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, said his next chapter would most likely include teaching or a fellowship.
Created by Congress as a trust in 1846, the Smithsonian has long been viewed as independent of the executive branch. Its governing Board of Regents must now appoint a new leader in the face of withering attacks from the administration.
The 17-person panel, led by Roberts, includes six members of Congress, split along party lines; nine private citizens; and Vice President JD Vance. The terms of three citizen members have recently expired, and the names of replacement nominees have not made it to Congress, an unusual holding pattern that appears to be evidence of the shadow war over control of the Smithsonian.
In the short term, Bunch seemed to have sufficient board support to stay on. But he has indicated that he is weary of the fray and ready for some form of retirement.
“When you’re Black in America, you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right?” he told The New York Times in May. “You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table. So in some ways, all of that prepared me for this moment.”
“But do I wish I was in it?” he continued, referring to scrutiny by the Trump administration. “Of course not. Good Lord, I wish that I was doing my goodbye tour.”
Over nearly 40 years in various roles at the Smithsonian, Bunch developed a reputation as a soft-spoken diplomat adept at raising money and dealing with public officials. As the institution’s first Black secretary, he has at times been a forceful voice on issues of race, particularly after the 2017 white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, and in the wake of George Floyd’s murder in Minneapolis in 2020.
Trump did not pay much attention to Washington’s cultural organizations in his first term but has made them a focus of his second, including through his efforts to govern, close and renovate the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The Smithsonian has been forced to respond to White House demands or risk potential cuts to its $1 billion budget, which is largely funded by the federal government.
Last month, in a letter to the board, Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, and Vince Haley, a senior White House adviser, made the stakes clear.
“The Smithsonian enjoys support from executive departments and agencies,” the letter said. “Those executive departments and agencies cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership.”
The president’s attempt to overhaul the Smithsonian began last year with an executive order that accused the institution of promoting “narratives that portray American and Western values as inherently harmful and oppressive” and called for an end to spending on exhibitions or programs that “degrade shared American values, divide Americans based on race or promote programs or ideologies inconsistent with federal law.”
After the White House demanded that the Smithsonian turn over information about the content of its exhibitions, Bunch reasserted the institution’s independence while saying that materials had been submitted in an effort to be “transparent.”
The board adopted a resolution that called for its 21 museums to review their content for partisanship or bias. But the administration began its own review of exhibitions, wall text and social media to assess “tone, historical framing and alignment with American ideals.”
Trump has been unrelenting in his criticism, posting on social media that “the Smithsonian is OUT OF CONTROL, where everything discussed is how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was, and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been — Nothing about Success, nothing about Brightness, nothing about the Future. We are not going to allow this to happen.”
The president also announced online that he was dismissing the director of the National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, calling her “a highly partisan person, and a strong supporter of DEI.” (The Smithsonian insisted it controlled personnel matters, but Sajet resigned, citing the institution’s best interests.)
The White House pressure reached a new pitch this year with a July 4 report about the National Museum of American History that accused its director of “radical activist ideology” and the museum of undermining “faith in American institutions.”
Many historians expressed serious concern about the report, but some conservatives applauded it, joining Trump in arguing that exhibits had become overly focused on race, identity and injustice.
“Hardworking Americans don’t want their taxpayer dollars dedicated to Marxist indoctrination,” Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, wrote on social media.
After the report, Anthea Hartig, the museum’s director, came under fire at two congressional hearings. Then Trump ordered warning signs and exhibits installed to convey his view that the museum did not accurately reflect American history. The signs have yet to materialize.
Bunch said it had been difficult to have his colleagues attacked by the administration. “I have always tried to protect people,” he said. “So I’ve always said, ‘Let the most of the weight fall on me. They don’t deserve it.’ We’re in a time when people are being hurt.”
His priority has been “How do I always make sure that we put the Smithsonian in the strongest position?” Bunch said. “That we articulate what we believe in, the importance of nonpartisanship and scholarship?”
When Bunch became the leader of the African American museum in 2005, that institution remained a distant dream.
He worked with Congress to fund it and attracted big-name donors including Oprah Winfrey. He appointed Republicans such as Laura Bush and Colin Powell to the board and won support by arguing that the museum should recognize the horrors of slavery and the struggle for civil rights while celebrating historical Black achievements. Bunch said the museum needed to tell “the quintessential American story” of progress.
It opened to great fanfare in 2016 and was the Smithsonian’s fourth-most-popular destination last year, with 1.6 million visitors. Bunch ascended to the Smithsonian’s top job in 2019.
In the spring, Bunch said he was proud of what the Smithsonian had achieved under his leadership despite the barrage of Trump attacks. “Nothing can take that away,” he said. “So I’m trying to make sure I don’t let this moment steal my joy.”
This week, he spoke of how important it was for the Smithsonian to continue to explore the country’s past in all its complexity. “Americans are an amazingly brave people, who have accomplished so much,” he said. “They’ve got to be brave enough to face their own history.”
“To me, that is essential,” he continued. “And I will stand against wind and tide to prevent history from being erased, softened and made palatable. That’s wrong.”

(WASHINGTON) — Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch is stepping down from his position, the institution said Tuesday, after seven years of leading the world’s largest museum, education and research complex.
“I have fought for as long as I can. I love this country and I love the Smithsonian and I will always work to defend our more perfect Union,” Bunch told ABC News in a statement, confirming his resignation on Tuesday.
Bunch’s resignation comes amid mounting attacks against the Smithsonian from the Trump administration, which has accused Smithsonian leadership of presenting a “radical view” of American history and threatening to withhold federal funds and support.
“It is with very mixed emotions and heartfelt gratitude that I announce my retirement from the Smithsonian,” Bunch said in a statement. “I have spent nearly half of my life working at and being part of the Smithsonian family, and what a privilege it has been. There is no place like the Smithsonian—it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together. I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.”
Bunch, who has been a part of the Smithsonian Institution for the past 38 years, was named secretary in June 2019, making him the first African American and first historian to serve in the role. Bunch did not reference the ongoing attacks from the White House in his parting statement.
“It is time for my next chapter, a chapter that will allow me to continue to protect the integrity of the Smithsonian and to champion the importance of a history that illuminates and celebrates the complex story of our nation,” Bunch said. “The Smithsonian has been a reservoir of science, history, art and culture that freely allows the public to find knowledge, understanding, clarity, education, hope and a bit of joy. I will always carry the Smithsonian within me.”
Bunch reflected on his legacy in a July interview with ABC News to mark America’s 250th birthday.
Asked about the White House’s criticism of the Smithsonian, Bunch said, “I think that for me it’s — I’m always open to any criticism, any comments. We want to be in the best institutions we can be.”
He added, “But I feel very strongly that a nation has to understand the totality of its past, the complexity of its past, in order to understand greatness of a nation.”
In July, the White House released a scathing 162-page report accusing the Smithsonian Institution of engaging in “extreme political activism” and presenting “a radical view of American history.”
The report, which was published by the White House Domestic Policy Council, took aim at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History (NMAH), accusing its leadership of adopting “an ideological framework that no longer treats the American story as a shared national inheritance to be taught or celebrated, but as a political instrument to divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens.”
The report came amid a review of the Smithsonian that was launched in response to President Donald Trump’s March 27, 2025, executive order, “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.”
The executive order directed Vice President J.D. Vance, in consultation with the president’s advisers on domestic policy, “to remove improper ideology” from Smithsonian institutions, arguing that materials that cast America in a “negative light” have no place in federal cultural institutions.
Amid escalating attacks from the White House, NMAH Director Anthea Hartig became the first Smithsonian official in July to testify on the issue before Congress.
In her testimony, Hartig pushed back against the White House July 4 report, asserting that the museum “does not take sides” in political debates.
“Our work is governed by the Smithsonian standards of scholarship, accuracy, independence, and nonpartisanship,” Hartig said in her opening remarks before a House Subcommittee on Delivering Government Efficiency. “The museum does not take sides in America’s political debates. We preserve and document the evidence of American life in all of its breadth, so that the public can encounter the past and draw their own conclusions.”
Bunch, who met with Trump at the White House last August, has repeatedly affirmed the Smithsonian’s “independence” from political influence.
Referencing his conversations with Trump in a September 2025 letter to the institution’s employees, Bunch underscored the independence of the Smithsonian, saying it was “paramount.” He also told employees that the institution remains committed to telling the “American story” and “will always be, a place that welcomes all Americans and the world.”
The Smithsonian is overseen by a 17-member governing body, known as the Board of Regents.
Franklin D. Raines, chair of the Board of Regents, said board members will announce an acting secretary as they begin a national search for Bunch’s successor.
“I have had the honor of working with Lonnie Bunch for more than two decades, first when he was the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture and ultimately when he became the 14th Secretary of the Smithsonian,” Raines said in a statement on Tuesday. “I have seen firsthand how Secretary Bunch’s leadership of our 21 museums and the National Zoo has illuminated the nation’s past, opened pathways to new knowledge and powered creativity and innovation.”
ABC News’ Kyra Phillips and John Santucci contributed to this report.

Bunch steps down after ‘stressful’ pressure from White House

Lonnie Bunch III, who led the charge to build the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture and formerly served as the Chicago History Museum president, will step down from his post as the 14th secretary of the Smithsonian, he said in a statement Tuesday.
A historian by training, Bunch became the first Black person and first historian appointed to the position atop the Smithsonian — the world’s largest museum — in June 2019. His efforts to maintain the museum’s independence amid an internal review initiated by President Donald Trump’s administration “to assess tone, historical framing, and alignment with American ideals” put him at odds with the president.
Bunch said in the statement Tuesday that he leaves the Smithsonian with “pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.” He plans to step down at the end of the year, The New York Times reported.
The secretary of the Smithsonian is responsible for 21 museums and 14 research centers.
Bunch, who ran the Chicago Historical Society (later renamed Chicago History Museum) from 2001 to 2005, was the driving force behind the creation of the Smithsonian National Museum of African American History. The $540 million project, which began during the administration of George W. Bush, opened in 2016 during the tenure of President Barack Obama.
Bunch told the Chicago Sun-Times in 2016 that his political dealings in Chicago — including with former Mayor Richard M. Daley, former Gov. George Ryan, the leaders of the Illinois General Assembly and Chicago’s corporate community — taught him “the power of a marriage that includes the corporate community, the political community and the cultural community.”
The D.C. museum featured many Chicago artifacts, including a Pullman porter cap, a pew from the Quinn Chapel AME Church and furniture from the set of Oprah Winfrey’s show.
Bunch told WBEZ’s Reset in October 2019 that he wanted to steward a project that told many viewpoints.
“One of the things that was so important was to realize there wasn’t a single African American experience,” he said. “So we really tell stories through the lens of Chicago or Birmingham so that people get a sense that this is an amazingly complicated community. But maybe the most important thing we do is all of those stories are done in a way that said this is not a separate story about the Black experience. It is really using the African American experience as a lens to understand what it means to be an American.”
Museums, he told Reset, should not just be backward-looking.
“I really do think that if the museum is just about yesterday, then it fails,” he said. “But if it helps us think about yesterday, today and tomorrow, then it becomes a place that is valued and contributes in a way to making a country better.”
Last summer, the White House issued an executive order titled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History” that initiated a review of the Smithsonian’s public-facing content, exhibition materials and curation process. The initial review focused on eight museums, including the National Museum of African American History and Culture, the National Museum of American History and the National Portrait Gallery.
The review, the White House said, was intended to “ensure alignment with Trump’s directive to celebrate American exceptionalism, remove divisive or partisan narratives, and restore confidence in our shared cultural institutions.”
A subsequent 162-page report by the Domestic Policy Council, issued in July, criticized the National Museum of American History and its director for “failing” to illuminate the nation’s heritage and displaying materials “intended to undermine faith in American institutions.”
In a memo, obtained by the Washington Post, Bunch defended the institution: “At the Smithsonian, our work is driven by scholarship, accuracy and an uncompromising commitment to tell the fullness of America’s story,” he wrote. “As public servants and the keepers of this institution, we are charged with helping a nation find understanding, hope and clarity and as part of that duty, we are dedicated to excellence, reflection and growth.”
Bunch told The New York Times it was not the pressure that had led to his resignation.
“It was really just saying, now’s the time.”

*Lonnie G. Bunch III, the Smithsonian Institution’s first Black secretary and the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, is retiring by the end of 2026 as President Donald Trump‘s administration intensifies its campaign to influence how the institution presents American history.
Bunch, 73, has led the Smithsonian since 2019. His departure after more than seven years in the top job arrives at an extraordinary moment: The White House has challenged Smithsonian exhibits and leadership over depictions of race, slavery and other difficult chapters of the nation’s past.
But Bunch says that fight is not why he’s leaving.
Why Bunch Says He’s Leaving
Bunch told The Washington Post that administration pressure “played no role” in his retirement decision. He said he had been considering leaving for about a year and reached his decision after spending several weeks this summer with his children and grandchildren.
“For, I don’t know, 45 years, work has taken precedence over family,” Bunch told the newspaper, explaining that at 73 he wants more years with his family.
That distinction matters. Bunch is leaving amid a political battle with the Trump administration, but his own account contradicts any suggestion that Trump forced him out.
The Wall Street Journal first reported his retirement Tuesday, describing his departure against the backdrop of escalating tensions with Trump.
Trump’s Smithsonian Fight Isn’t Over
The conflict surrounding Bunch’s final months is substantial. A July 2026 Trump executive order accused Smithsonian leadership of failing to present American history as a shared national inheritance and directed federal officials to use available authority to encourage changes at the institution. The White House order followed an earlier Trump directive attacking what the administration called “divisive, race-centered ideology.”
Bunch, meanwhile, has defended the Smithsonian’s independence.
“We’re at a time when people are challenging that independence,” he told The Post, adding that he would continue fighting for it as long as he remained secretary.
From Black History Museum to Smithsonian Leader
Bunch’s departure carries particular weight because of his role in bringing Black history into one of America’s most prominent cultural institutions.
He was the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, which opened in 2016, before becoming the first African American and first historian to lead the Smithsonian.
EURweb previously covered Bunch when he received the NAACP President’s Award for his work establishing the museum and creating a national institution honoring African American contributions. EURweb’s earlier coverage of Bunch
What Happens After Bunch?
Bunch’s retirement therefore closes one chapter while leaving a much larger question unresolved: who will lead the Smithsonian through its continuing confrontation with the Trump administration?
The Smithsonian’s Board of Regents—not the president—selects the secretary. Bunch told The Post he intends to remain long enough to help ensure an orderly transition.
He may be ready to spend more time with his grandchildren, but the argument surrounding the institution he leaves behind—over independence, scholarship and who gets to tell America’s complicated history—is nowhere near retirement.

Less than three weeks ago in Philadelphia, Lonnie G. Bunch III, as 14th secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, was surrounded by people who had devoted their careers to preserving Black history at the Association of African American Museums’ 48th annual conference Aug. 19-21.
Then, he said, “I’m doing the best I can,” at a moment when the country’s most powerful museum system was facing extraordinary pressure from the White House over what Americans should be told about their past.
On Tuesday, Bunch announced his retirement from his post and ending his tenure as the first African American secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, a role that requires him to oversee 21 museums, the National Zoo, research centers and more.
“I have spent nearly half of my life working at and being part of the Smithsonian family, and what a privilege it has been,” Bunch wrote, according to Smithsonian Magazine. “There is no place like the Smithsonian—it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together.”
In a statement, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, said that Bunch had “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story” and that the Smithsonian had “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership.” The Smithsonian said Mr. Bunch was expected to depart at the end of the year.
His departure comes after more than a year of escalating pressure from President Donald Trump and his administration over the Smithsonian’s treatment of slavery, race, immigration and other parts of American history. Trump has accused the institution of presenting the country too negatively, while his administration has demanded reviews of museum exhibitions and materials and accused the National Museum of American History of political activism.
Bunch repeatedly defended the Smithsonian without turning his disagreements with the White House into a personal fight with Trump.
“It scares me when people aren’t brave enough to face their history,” Bunch said during a television interview this summer.
The sentence captured much of the philosophy that guided Bunch through four decades in museums. History, in his telling, was never supposed to comfort everyone who encountered it. Nor was it meant to indict the country. Its value came from presenting enough of the truth for Americans to understand both what their nation had accomplished and whom it had failed.
“We try to tell a complicated story that is driven by the best nonpartisan scholarship we have,” Bunch said in another television interview as criticism from the administration intensified.
Bunch vs. Trump
The conflict had been building since Trump’s return to office in 2025. Trump signed an executive order in March of that year accusing the Smithsonian of advancing narratives that portray American and Western values as “inherently harmful and oppressive.” The White House later began reviewing exhibitions and materials at several Smithsonian museums.
By July 2026, the fight was no longer confined to bureaucratic correspondence.
A 162-page White House report accused the National Museum of American History of “extreme political activism” and said the museum had turned history into an instrument to “divide, dispirit and discourage” Americans. Bunch responded in a message to Smithsonian employees that the report was “not a fair characterization” of the museum’s work.
Trump later ordered warning signs placed at the National Museum of American History telling visitors that the museum did not, in his administration’s view, accurately portray the country’s history.
Then, days before Bunch’s departure, the administration increased the pressure again. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and White House Domestic Policy Council Director Vince Haley warned that federal agencies could withdraw cooperation with the Smithsonian under its current leadership, including artifact loans, procurement assistance and discretionary grants.
“It is also concerning that the Smithsonian leadership’s culture of ideological activism has not only corrupted the Institution but has spread across the country and corrupted the American Alliance for Museums- the primary organization and accrediting body for the museum profession-among others,” they wrote in an Aug. 26 letter.
For Bunch, the fight reached the institution whose very existence became inseparable from his name.
When he became founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture in July 2005, there was no museum.
There was one employee. No building, no collection, no site, and no substantial pool of money to make the dream real.
Bunch spent the next 11 years changing that.
The museum, which finally opened beside the Washington Monument in September 2016, became one of Washington’s most sought-after destinations. Its collection grew to roughly 40,000 objects, preserving everything from the brutality of slavery and segregation to Black achievement in politics, music, sports, military service, business and culture.
Nearly 13 million people have visited since its opening.
Bunch later described his improbable assignment in the title of his book, “A Fool’s Errand: Creating the National Museum of African American History and Culture in the Age of Bush, Obama, and Trump.”
“So many experiences throughout my career had prepared me and positioned me for this, the grandest challenge of my life, what some have labeled my calling,” Bunch wrote in the 2019 book, according to an excerpt printed by CBS News.

The museum also made Bunch something rare in Washington: a historian whose work crossed presidential administrations and partisan lines.
President George W. Bush appointed him to the Committee for the Preservation of the White House in 2002. President Barack Obama reappointed him in 2010. The African American museum itself resulted from decades of advocacy and ultimately opened with Bush and Obama participating in its dedication.
Three years later, in June 2019, Bunch became the Smithsonian’s 14th secretary. He assumed responsibility for 21 museums, 21 libraries, the National Zoo, research centers and educational operations, while overseeing development of the National Museum of the American Latino and the Smithsonian American Women’s History Museum.
His résumé reaches well beyond Washington.
Bunch led the Chicago Historical Society from 2001 to 2005 and previously worked at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, where he rose to associate director for curatorial affairs. Earlier, at the California African American Museum in Los Angeles, he curated exhibitions on Black Olympians and Black life in Los Angeles.
The Belleville, New Jersey, native earned his undergraduate and graduate degrees from American University in Washington, and taught at American University, George Washington University, and the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth.
His honors include France’s Legion of Honor, the W.E.B. Du Bois Medal, the Freedom Medal from the Roosevelt Institute, the NAACP Legal Defense Fund’s National Equal Justice Award and lifetime achievement awards from the American Alliance of Museums and the Association of African American Museums.
Yet the institution that will define his career sits on Constitution Avenue.
Just eight days before Tuesday’s announcement, Bunch published a remembrance of building the African American history museum for its 10th anniversary. He recalled the September 2016 dedication, when four generations of the Bonner family rang a church bell once owned by a Black congregation founded in 1776.
Ruth Bonner, then 99— whose father had been born enslaved— pulled the rope alongside her 7-year-old great-granddaughter.
Bunch wrote that he could still remember looking across the Mall years earlier at the empty patch of land where the museum would eventually rise.
“Ten years on,” he wrote, “I feel the same.”
The battle surrounding the Smithsonian is ultimately about the subject that defined Bunch’s professional life — who gets remembered, what gets displayed and whether the ugliest chapters of American history belong beside its triumphs.
Bunch addressed that question as the United States celebrated its 250th anniversary.
“It’s really important that we have a commitment to telling the complete story of America,” he said. “Our job is to say, how do we tell an accurate history … that challenges America to live up to its ideals?”
A decade earlier, as the African American history museum finally opened, Bunch stood on the National Mall and listened as former President George W. Bush offered a sentence that now follows Bunch out of the institution he led.
“A great nation does not hide its history,” Bush demanded.
Ten years later, Bunch is stepping down, having not only witnessed the success of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, but also served as a barrier-breaker.

sources.text:
After a seven-year run marked most recently by attacks from the Trump administration, Lonnie Bunch III announced Tuesday that he was stepping down as secretary of the Smithsonian.
The White House has escalated its criticism of how the Smithsonian presents American history and values, prompting concern from some about what they see as an assault on the institution’s autonomy and commendation from others for reining in an organization they view as overtaken by liberal bias.
In an interview, Bunch, 73, said it was not the pressure that had led to his departure.
“It was really just saying, now’s the time,” he said.
“I’m a fighter,” he added.
At the same time, he acknowledged the strain of the role.
“I have to be honest, it has been stressful,” he said. “And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”
In a statement, Chief Justice John Roberts, who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, said that Bunch had “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story” and that the Smithsonian had “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership.” The Smithsonian said Bunch was expected to depart at the end of the year.
For more than a year, Bunch has tried to balance diplomacy and openness to criticism with a determination to resist a White House push to present what President Donald Trump calls “patriotic” history. Some admire how Bunch has managed to quietly hold the line against the White House. Others believe the Smithsonian has shown too much deference to Trump and even engaged in self-censorship.
Last year, painter Amy Sherald withdrew her blockbuster show at the National Portrait Gallery over a disagreement about how the museum would display her portrait of a transgender Statue of Liberty.
But Bunch said he had no regrets. “My goal has been to win, not to make me feel good,” he said. “To win — to protect the Smithsonian — there were times I would fight, make clear what the red lines were. And there were other times I let things go.”
Bunch, a widely respected historian who previously oversaw the creation of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, said his next chapter would most likely include teaching or a fellowship.
Created by Congress as a trust in 1846, the Smithsonian has long been viewed as independent of the executive branch. Its governing Board of Regents must now appoint a new leader in the face of withering attacks from the administration.
The 17-person panel, led by Roberts, includes six members of Congress, split along party lines; nine private citizens; and Vice President JD Vance. The terms of three citizen members have recently expired, and the names of replacement nominees have not made it to Congress, an unusual holding pattern that appears to be evidence of the shadow war over control of the Smithsonian.
In the short term, Bunch seemed to have sufficient board support to stay on. But he has indicated that he is weary of the fray and ready for some form of retirement.
“When you’re Black in America, you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right?” he told The New York Times in May. “You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table. So in some ways, all of that prepared me for this moment.”
“But do I wish I was in it?” he continued, referring to scrutiny by the Trump administration. “Of course not. Good Lord, I wish that I was doing my goodbye tour.”
Over nearly 40 years in various roles at the Smithsonian, Bunch developed a reputation as a soft-spoken diplomat adept at raising money and dealing with public officials. As the institution’s first Black secretary, he has at times been a forceful voice on issues of race, particularly after the 2017 white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, and in the wake of George Floyd’s murder in Minneapolis in 2020.
Trump did not pay much attention to Washington’s cultural organizations in his first term but has made them a focus of his second, including through his efforts to govern, close and renovate the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The Smithsonian has been forced to respond to White House demands or risk potential cuts to its $1 billion budget, which is largely funded by the federal government.
Last month, in a letter to the board, Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, and Vince Haley, a senior White House adviser, made the stakes clear.
“The Smithsonian enjoys support from executive departments and agencies,” the letter said. “Those executive departments and agencies cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership.”
The president’s attempt to overhaul the Smithsonian began last year with an executive order that accused the institution of promoting “narratives that portray American and Western values as inherently harmful and oppressive” and called for an end to spending on exhibitions or programs that “degrade shared American values, divide Americans based on race or promote programs or ideologies inconsistent with federal law.”
After the White House demanded that the Smithsonian turn over information about the content of its exhibitions, Bunch reasserted the institution’s independence while saying that materials had been submitted in an effort to be “transparent.”
The board adopted a resolution that called for its 21 museums to review their content for partisanship or bias. But the administration began its own review of exhibitions, wall text and social media to assess “tone, historical framing and alignment with American ideals.”
Trump has been unrelenting in his criticism, posting on social media that “the Smithsonian is OUT OF CONTROL, where everything discussed is how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was, and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been -- Nothing about Success, nothing about Brightness, nothing about the Future. We are not going to allow this to happen.”
The president also announced online that he was dismissing the director of the National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, calling her “a highly partisan person, and a strong supporter of DEI.” (The Smithsonian insisted it controlled personnel matters, but Sajet resigned, citing the institution’s best interests.)
The White House pressure reached a new pitch this year with a July 4 report about the National Museum of American History that accused its director of “radical activist ideology” and the museum of undermining “faith in American institutions.”
Many historians expressed serious concern about the report, but some conservatives applauded it, joining Trump in arguing that exhibits had become overly focused on race, identity and injustice.
“Hardworking Americans don’t want their taxpayer dollars dedicated to Marxist indoctrination,” Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, wrote on social media.
After the report, Anthea Hartig, the museum’s director, came under fire at two congressional hearings. Then Trump ordered warning signs and exhibits installed to convey his view that the museum did not accurately reflect American history. The signs have yet to materialize.
Bunch said it had been difficult to have his colleagues attacked by the administration. “I have always tried to protect people,” he said. “So I’ve always said, ‘Let the most of the weight fall on me. They don’t deserve it.’ We’re in a time when people are being hurt.”
His priority has been “How do I always make sure that we put the Smithsonian in the strongest position?” Bunch said. “That we articulate what we believe in, the importance of nonpartisanship and scholarship?”
When Bunch became the leader of the African American museum in 2005, that institution remained a distant dream.
He worked with Congress to fund it and attracted big-name donors including Oprah Winfrey. He appointed Republicans such as Laura Bush and Colin Powell to the board and won support by arguing that the museum should recognize the horrors of slavery and the struggle for civil rights while celebrating historical Black achievements. Bunch said the museum needed to tell “the quintessential American story” of progress.
It opened to great fanfare in 2016 and was the Smithsonian’s fourth-most-popular destination last year, with 1.6 million visitors. Bunch ascended to the Smithsonian’s top job in 2019.
In the spring, Bunch said he was proud of what the Smithsonian had achieved under his leadership despite the barrage of Trump attacks. “Nothing can take that away,” he said. “So I’m trying to make sure I don’t let this moment steal my joy.”
This week, he spoke of how important it was for the Smithsonian to continue to explore the country’s past in all its complexity. “Americans are an amazingly brave people, who have accomplished so much,” he said. “They’ve got to be brave enough to face their own history.”
“To me, that is essential,” he continued. “And I will stand against wind and tide to prevent history from being erased, softened and made palatable. That’s wrong.”

Bunch, 73, has earned a reputation as a historian unafraid of confronting some of the darkest period's in U.S. history and an adept political operator who maintained strong bipartisan support during his tenure.
Bunch has served the Smithsonian Institution for 38 years and oversaw some of the Smithsonian's most ambitious projects, including the construction of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, which he founded.
Supreme Court Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who serves as the head of the Board of Regents, said Bunch "pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story” and the institution “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision, and leadership.”
“We look forward to working with him in the coming months to ensure a smooth transition for his successor,” Roberts said in a statement.
President Donald Trump has previously praised Bunch for his enthusiasm for his role leading the nation's flagship museum system.
"I am very, very proud of Lonnie Bunch," he said in 2017 during remarks at the National Museum of African American History and Culture.

Trump signed an executive order in March 2025 titled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History," objecting to what he called a concerted effort to downplay American successes, and to cast historical milestones and the nation's founding principles "in a negative light."

Bunch, 73, said in multiple interviews that his retirement was not related to pressure from the Trump administration to make changes to the institution.

CNN has reached out to the White House for comment.

Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III Announces Retirement as Head of the Smithsonian After 38 Years of Service to the Institution
With a storied career dating back to the 1970s, Bunch leaves a remarkable legacy, most notably the founding of the National Museum of African American History and Culture
In a statement issued today, Lonnie G. Bunch III announced his retirement after seven years as the 14th Secretary of the Smithsonian. “I have spent nearly half of my life working at and being part of the Smithsonian family, and what a privilege it has been,” he wrote. “There is no place like the Smithsonian—it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together. I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.”
Bunch was named to the role by the Smithsonian Board of Regents in 2019, having most recently served as the founding director of the Institution’s National Museum of African American History and Culture (NMAAHC).
In a press release, the Institution wrote that details of the leadership transition will be announced at a later date. Bunch will serve in the role through the end of the year, according to the New York Times. The Board of Regents, composed of legislators from across Congress, in addition to civilian members, holds the responsibility of electing the next leader of the Smithsonian. Chief Justice of the United States John Roberts, who also serves as the chancellor of the Smithsonian, said in the release, “The Regents, and the Smithsonian, have benefited greatly from [Secretary Bunch’s] wisdom, vision and leadership. We look forward to working with him in the coming months to ensure a smooth transition for his successor.”
In the release, Bunch also wrote, “It is time for my next chapter, a chapter that will allow me to continue to protect the integrity of the Smithsonian and to champion the importance of a history that illuminates and celebrates the complex story of our nation.”
Quick facts: Lonnie Bunch, the early years
- 
	Bunch was born in Newark, New Jersey, and grew up in nearby Belleville.
- 
	He attended Howard University before transferring to American University, where he earned his B.A., M.A. and PhD in American history.
Bunch’s tenure as Smithsonian Secretary was marked by the addition of two new members to the Institution’s existing roster of 19 museums: the Smithsonian American Women’s History Museum and the National Museum of the American Latino. Just last month, the Smithsonian announced that the latter museum would take over the historic Arts and Industries Building on the National Mall as its permanent home.
Bunch also oversaw a massive digital-first transformation of the Institution. In an interview with Smithsonian magazine on his first day as Secretary, Bunch said, “We have the most amazing assets—our scholarship, our collections, the history of what we’ve done. How would we reinvent that in a world without bricks and mortar?” This shift bore fruit during the Covid-19 pandemic, as Americans looked to trusted sources like the Smithsonian for information. When Bunch was growing up in New Jersey as the child of two teachers, he wrote in 2020, his parents ingrained in him the importance of education, a lesson he brought to the Institution’s pandemic initiatives: “Committing to our educational mission means reaching people where they are by increasing our digital resources, working with school districts to develop effective distance learning tools, supporting educators and families in an unfamiliar situation.”
Bunch began his career at the Institution in the late 1970s, when Apollo 11 astronaut and National Air and Space Museum director Michael Collins hired him to work in the education department. Even though he had dreams of teaching at a university, Bunch realized that he could have a much greater impact with the “national classroom” of the Smithsonian. “My time there was the most life-changing thing I’ve ever experienced professionally,” he recently said.
He left the Smithsonian for a teaching role at the University of Massachusetts and then served as the first curator at the California African American Museum in Los Angeles before returning to the National Mall in 1989 with a curatorial role at the National Museum of American History. There, he collected one of the Institution’s iconic artifacts, the Greensboro Lunch Counter, and curated the still-popular exhibition on the American presidency.
He left the Smithsonian once again to lead the Chicago History Museum, before returning one last time as the founding director of NMAAHC, which opened in 2016. In an interview earlier this year, Bunch looked back on the arduous, yet fulfilling, time of building a museum literally from the ground up. “There's no doubt that it was the high point of my career. When I became Secretary, somebody said, ‘Oh, this is the capstone of your career.’ No, I already did that. This is OK, but no, I already did that.”
In 2025, Bunch said in an interview with Smithsonian, “One of the reasons I agreed to become Secretary years ago was because of my profound respect for the amazing work of my colleagues.” He added that the Smithsonian “is a collection of amazing people who do work that sometimes is not understood, sometimes that is undervalued, but it’s work that as Secretary, I see as essential to a nation understanding itself.”
